item.title: Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss

In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).

Published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar, the study found that the percentage of patients with overweight or obesity and without type 2 diabetes who filled prescriptions for semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound) within six months of becoming eligible surged from 1.9% in 2021 to 16.6% in 2025.

But prescriptions for these medications were lower among men, Black or Hispanic patients, younger or older patients (ages 18–34 or 55–64), patients in a lower BMI category and/or patients whose health care provider was located in a neighborhood with lower socioeconomic status (SES), measured by education levels in the provider's ZIP code.

These disparities widened over time and were particularly pronounced in 2024 and 2025, after semaglutide and tirzepatide received formal approval by the Food and Drug Administration for chronic weight management in 2021 and 2023, respectively.

By mimicking a natural hormone that helps regulate insulin, blood sugar, appetite and digestion, GLP-1s can help people achieve dramatic weight loss, particularly those who struggle to lose weight through traditional diet and exercise. Health experts worry that persistent challenges with GLP-1 accessibility and affordability are hindering large swaths of eligible people from receiving life-changing and potentially lifesaving treatment.

"Our study focuses on a population that is especially vulnerable to inequities in GLP-1 access," says study senior author Dr. Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at BUSPH, who studies population health, aging and mortality, including inequities in GLP-1 access.

"We have better treatments for obesity than ever, but access to them hasn't caught up. It is much easier for people with diabetes to get these drugs covered by insurance. But for people living with overweight or obesity, coverage is very difficult to obtain—even when they qualify—because providers and insurers don't always view these as conditions that merit treatment. This is a population that has been left behind."

As these medications continue to gain prominence, the findings underscore the need for health care providers to receive appropriate training and resources about prescribing GLP-1 treatments, as well as the need for improvements in insurance companies' drug benefit design to ensure that people who qualify for these treatments can easily access them.

"GLP-1 receptor agonists are moving into routine care very quickly, but without deliberate action, these drugs risk widening the health inequities that obesity already reflects," says study lead and corresponding author Dr. Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst in the Department of Global Health at BUSPH at the time of the study.

Stokes and Le utilized medical claims data from a national database that includes closed claims for more than 175 million patients. For the analysis, they examined health information, GLP-1 treatment and health care provider locations among 512,389 eligible, commercially insured patients ages 18–64. The analysis did not include patients covered by Medicaid or Medicare, people without insurance or prescriptions obtained through direct-to-consumer channels.

Despite the nearly ninefold rise in GLP-1 prescriptions among eligible patients during the study period, the researchers point out that the vast majority of eligible patients still do not receive these prescriptions for weight management. People with employer-sponsored and other commercial insurance are more likely to have access to GLP-1s.

That racial disparities in access to these medications were still evident among the study's commercially insured participants underscores the long-standing structural barriers to health care that Black and Hispanic patients experience, even as they are burdened by obesity and other health conditions at greater rates than other populations. Black and Hispanic patients are more likely to face biases and stigma in health care, mistrust of the health care system and higher medication costs, all of which can exacerbate racial disparities in GLP-1 uptake.

The expansion in GLP-1 medication use also disproportionately benefited patients who saw providers in higher-SES neighborhoods. These SES disparities were smaller in the beginning of the study period but widened over time and were larger among patients in lower BMI categories. These disparities were also particularly pronounced among men, which the researchers say may reflect men's lower likelihood of seeking weight-management care.

"Patients seen at clinics in lower socioeconomic neighborhoods had about 35% lower odds of being prescribed semaglutide or tirzepatide in 2024–2025; early on, that gap was about 15%," says Le. Insurance coverage alone doesn't close the gap, he says. "We need to look at how drug benefits are designed, including prior authorization, step therapy and out-of-pocket costs that land unevenly on different patients. We also need to give under-resourced practices real support, such as help with prior-authorization paperwork, so that a clinic's administrative capacity doesn't decide who gets treated."…

item.title: Giving patients a greater voice in their diabetes care
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Giving patients a greater voice in their diabetes care

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

In two related papers published in JAMA Network Open and the Journal of General Internal Medicine, Kasia Lipska, M.D., associate professor of medicine (endocrinology) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and her colleagues tested a new approach to incorporating patients' priorities into their diabetes care.

"What matters most to someone living with diabetes doesn't always make it into the clinic visit," says Lipska. "When a patient with diabetes comes into the office, we often start with their A1C, and then the whole conversation revolves around glycemic control." A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over roughly three months and helps clinicians decide whether to adjust a patient's diabetes medications.

"When blood sugar becomes the focus of the entire visit, it can leave little time or space to explore what else is going on in a patient's life," she adds.

To give patients more say in those conversations, Lipska and her team developed QBSAFE, a set of 14 conversation cards addressing different aspects of life with diabetes and its treatment. Each card contains a statement about topics such as quality of life, the demands of managing diabetes or concerns about treatment safety and complications. Before a visit, patients choose up to three cards highlighting issues they want to discuss, helping set the agenda for their care.

"Diabetes is a chronic condition that requires a lot of work to manage. We see a lot of people who are overwhelmed by their care—the medications, injections, blood sugar monitoring, diet, physical activity and appointments," says Lipska. "That's partly what the conversation cards are designed to allow us to talk about."

The team developed the cards based on research into common issues affecting quality of life for people with diabetes, along with patient feedback. Statements range from "I am frustrated by the amount of time I spend managing my diabetes" to "I find it hard to follow your suggestions about diet and exercise." Others highlight positive experiences, including "I have felt moments of pride while managing my diabetes."

"The cards aren't too prescriptive. They are just conversation starters," says Lipska. "And because they have statements rather than questions, they normalized things that may be more difficult for people to talk about."

The researchers examined how clinic visits and patient outcomes with the cards compared with usual care.

During visits, the cards prompted more conversations about the burdens of managing diabetes, including taking medications, following diet and exercise recommendations and navigating challenging life circumstances.

These are issues that can shape whether a patient can follow a care plan in the first place, says Lipska. Bringing them into the conversation gives clinicians a fuller picture of what patients are being asked to manage and gives patients an opening to explain where they need help.

Importantly, says Lipska, those conversations happened without lengthening visits or reducing attention to blood sugar control, suggesting clinicians can address both patients' daily challenges and their blood sugar goals within the same visit. At six months, clinician satisfaction and patient medication adherence were also higher in the QBSAFE group.

The next step is to help clinicians act on what they learn, says Lipska. Although the cards alone did not significantly improve blood sugar control, treatment burden, diabetes distress or illness intrusiveness over six months, the research team hopes to develop tools and training that will help clinicians simplify care and improve those outcomes.

"This goes beyond just algorithmic medicine," says Lipska. "We're trying to help clinicians think, troubleshoot and brainstorm with their patients to provide the best care."

Ultimately, Lipska hopes the work encourages a broader view of what successful diabetes management looks like.

"A1C and continuous glucose monitoring give us valuable information to care for people," she says. "But life is more than just measuring a glucose level—it's about overall health, quality of life and people's relationships. It's all those things."

Publication details

Kasia J. Lipska et al., A Conversation Tool to Enhance Care for People With Type 2 Diabetes, JAMA Network Open (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.39032

Victor Montori V et al., Videographic Analysis of an Intervention to Improve Patient-Centered Care for People Living with Type 2 Diabetes: The QBSAFE Randomized Trial, Journal of General Internal Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1007/s11606-026-10849-x

Journal information: JAMA Network Open , Journal of General Internal Medicine

item.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

- Published

Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.

Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.

Here's what you need to know.

UK blind to how quickly Covid was spreading

The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than Â£30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

But it didn't need to be like that

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.

Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.

This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.

They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.

Many self-isolating 'felt forgotten'

When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.

In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.

Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to Â£10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.

Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.

But it was not until September in England â and later in Scotland and Wales â that Â£500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.

More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Flights and borders - the mistakes

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.

The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."

By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.

By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".

Smart phones and the 'pingdemic'

The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".

It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.

Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.

It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible â and people have confidence in them.

In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".

It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

item.title: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.

The Conversation asked Dr. Andrew Wolf, a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the lead authors of the new guidelines, to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.

What are the new screening recommendations?

The biggest change is that we are making a proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer. Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.

Our new recommendations vary by age and by a person’s risk of developing prostate cancer.

For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.

People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.

For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, decision-making around screening depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy.

For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group.

Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is less effective than the PSA test. The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.

Why were the screening guidelines updated?

The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer.

The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer or of being diagnosed with metastatic disease are actually greater than researchers previously thought.

At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including false positive PSA test results and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are unlikely to harm patients in the long-term.

Who is most at risk for prostate cancer?

Black men have an approximately two-thirds higher risk of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors.

Men with a family history of prostate cancer in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk.

There are also a number of genetic mutations, such as BRCA2, that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American Urological Association, have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations.

Why has the PSA test been so controversial?

For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, a U.S. study, found no benefit to screening; the other, a European study, found only a relatively small benefit.

However, it later became clear that the U.S. study was seriously flawed in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up.

Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening.

After researchers followed patients for over two decades in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer.

This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as mammography for breast cancer. And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.

Why are there differences in guidelines?

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s last update in 2018, it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.…

item.title: Opinion: When should medical school start?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.

To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.

The story

“Medical school should start after students take the Step 1 exam,” by Rachel E. Fabi and Amy Caruso Brown

The response

The authors’ proposal hinges on the premise that learning the foundational sciences and learning to become a physician can be separated without compromising either. My first year of medical school was peppered with clinical exposure and taught me otherwise. I floundered with a blood pressure cuff during a wellness visit, fumbled for words as I interviewed a man waiting for a heart transplant, and listened to a patient recount her immense sorrow after multiple miscarriages. These encounters remain among my most formative.

I agree with the authors that students are often preoccupied with medical licensure exams, and that early clinical exposure might not cure this. In my experience, however, it is the strongest counterweight. After meeting those patients, I was learning for more than an exam. The proposed model would abandon that counterweight. Students would still encounter patients eventually, but we would have forfeited valuable time. Becoming a compassionate, humanistic physician is slow work, and it deserves all the time we can offer. A flashcard can teach a student what causes a miscarriage. It takes a patient to teach what it means to grieve one. And that lesson should not wait until after Step 1.

— Surya Pulukuri, Harvard Medical School student

The story

“The economics of the U.S. health care system are broken,” by Paul Markovich

The response

Markovich is correct: The U.S. health care “non-system” is broken. There are many culprits, including hospitals, whose prices are set more by market dominance than by quality. He should also look at the administrative complexity driven largely by our myriad of private insurance companies. Some 25% of U.S. “health care” spending goes to administrative costs. The insurers need to agree on a single set of billing codes and procedures to cut doctors’ and hospitals’ cost of billing. They need to sit down with doctors and come up with a uniform set of procedures needing pre-authorization and a single set of criteria. They need to agree on a small number of policy options that are understandable to the public. Finger-pointing is easy, but should start at home.

— Edward Hoffer, M.D., Harvard Medical School

The story

“Could long-term AI use lead to isolation? We need to find out — but researchers need better access to data,” by Qian Yang, Ned Cooper, and Ibrahim Emara

The response

A chatbot can handle every conversation responsibly and still, over time, take the place of someone a person used to confide in. In their First Opinion essay, Qian Yang, Ned Cooper, and Ibrahim Emara show how easily a gradual loss of human connection can escape safeguards designed for individual conversations. They make a persuasive case for giving independent researchers access to platform data and developing tools to distinguish the effects of chatbot use from other causes of isolation. Those tools should ask whether people could reach someone they trusted when they needed help.

That question is especially worth asking adolescents, who may have fewer ways to seek help privately. Imagine two teenagers who each spend an hour every night talking to a chatbot. One used to call a friend during difficult times, but he called less often as talking to the chatbot became a habit. The other still talks to friends every day. When she wanted to discuss something she feared would get back to her parents, she asked to see a school counselor. While she waited for an appointment, she took the problem to a chatbot. Their chat logs might look very similar. The authors suggest measuring school counselor time as one way to estimate what isolation costs schools. That measure captures time counselors spend helping students. Hours, days, or weeks spent waiting leave no trace.

Researchers could ask teens to think about the last time something was troubling them. Did they talk to someone about it, try to reach someone, or decide against reaching out? If they tried, did they get to talk to someone? Did they talk to a chatbot about it?

Asking these questions regularly could help researchers distinguish a teen who reached out to people less often as their chatbot usage grew from one who turned to a chatbot only after trying to get help. The distinction matters for policymaking. When chatbot use displaces human contact, usage limits may help. When it fills a gap in support, the priority should be making help easier to reach. A usage limit might prompt one teenager to call a friend. Another may still be waiting for someone to call back.

— Brian J. Carter, J.D., Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

item.title: Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper

The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.

The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.

For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.

The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.

While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.

Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.

All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.

The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.

Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.

Calls to investigate

A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.

"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."

The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.

A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.

"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

'Very sorry'

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.

Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.

But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.

The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.

A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.

"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

Clarification 20 November: This article was amended on 19 November to remove references to the information being 'leaked'. The information was mistakenly disclosed by the GMC in response to a media request.
